# KL2009 `writable-root-filesystem`

A container does not set `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`.

Category: `security`. Severity: `warning`. Disabled by default, select it by code or name to run it.

## What it does

Reports a container in `containers`, `initContainers` or `ephemeralContainers` whose
`securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem` is not `true`, either because it is `false` or
because it is not set. Kubernetes has no pod-level default for this field, so every
container must set it. Containers of Windows pods (`spec.os.name: windows`) are skipped,
because Kubernetes rejects the field there.

This rule is off by default: many images write to their own filesystem (caches, PID
files, temporary files) and need extra volumes before they can run read only. Enable it
with `--select KL2009` or in `kubelint.toml`.

## Why it matters

A writable root filesystem lets an attacker who gets code execution in the container
drop tools, change binaries or configuration, and persist until the container
restarts. A read-only root filesystem makes the image immutable at run time, so the
container runs exactly what was built and reviewed. Writes that the application really
needs go to explicit volumes, which also makes them visible in the manifest.

## Example

```yaml
containers:
- name: web
  image: nginx:1.27
```

Use instead:

```yaml
containers:
- name: web
  image: nginx:1.27
  securityContext:
    readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
  volumeMounts:
  - name: cache
    mountPath: /var/cache/nginx
volumes:
- name: cache
  emptyDir: {}
```
